#5795. Elizabeth Holmes Documentary: Doctors Weigh In

— MedPage Today reporters offer further insights into recently covered topics

The following is a transcript of the podcast episode:

Rachael Robertson: Hey everybody! Welcome to MedPod Today, the podcast series where MedPage Today reporters share deeper insight into the week's biggest healthcare stories. I'm your host, Rachael Robertson.

To kick things off, our perspectives editor Jenny Friedman will be talking about some recent op-eds about Nathan Fielder's documentary "You Can See Everything," which is about the disgraced Theranos CEO Elizabeth Holmes. Some medical organizations have really similar names but very different politics. Cheryl Clark will walk us through some of these groups that would be easy to confuse for each other. To close out, Kristina Fiore will share her reporting on a fluke that occurred during an internal medicine exam that has many test-takers frustrated.

Audiences have been flocking to theaters to see "You Can See Everything," which is Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim's new documentary about Elizabeth Holmes.

To refresh your memory, Holmes is the disgraced former CEO of blood testing company Theranos. She was convicted of defrauding investors and sentenced to 11 years in prison. The documentary places Fielder in the home of Holmes and her partner Billy Evans just 34 days before she is set to start her prison sentence. The film explores the question: Who is Elizabeth Holmes really?

Let me just share a few seconds of the trailer to set the scene.

Nathan Fielder: You really feel you did nothing wrong.

Fielder: So where did things get lost? Like how are you where you are right now?

Robertson: Perspectives editor Jenny Friedman has published a couple op-eds on the documentary, and she's here to discuss them.

So, Jenny, I understand we published two op-eds from doctors sharing their takeaways from the documentary. Are they taking a renewed look at the consequences of the Theranos scandal and Holmes' conviction?

Jenny Friedman: Not exactly. The intent of the documentary isn't to renegotiate Holmes's guilt; a jury and judge have already done that. The film also isn't trying to re-examine the consequences for investors or patients. Instead, the purpose is to paint a portrait of Holmes's psychology and let viewers decide for themselves what's real and what's fake. That fits really well into filmmaker Nathan Fielder's standard M.O. of blurring the lines between reality and fiction.

So, in one of our op-eds, a forensic psychiatrist, Susan Hatters Friedman, MD, draws from her clinical experience of working with women convicted of fraud in order to analyze the version of Holmes who we see on screen, and she offers insight into certain traits and behaviors that Holmes portrays. But she reminds readers and viewers, to keep in mind the collateral evidence of what we already know about Theranos and the conviction of Holmes. And if you recall, the evidence is overwhelming.

Robertson: Right. I mean, that's fascinating and really impressive that she was able to do that while also abiding by the Goldwater Rule. What's the second op-ed about?

Friedman: The other op-ed, written by psychiatry resident Chloe Lee, MD, MPH, looks at the relationship dynamics portrayed on screen between Holmes and her partner Billy Evans. And some viewers might leave the movie thinking of Holmes as the victim because on screen she plays a doting mother, while Evans exhibits controlling behaviors. But is that really her, or is she capable of manipulating a partner's abusive tendencies to her advantage? Those are the primary questions that psychiatry resident Chloe Lee is trying to address in her op-ed. And while Dr. Lee, like the rest of us moviegoers, can only see what's displayed on screen, she highlights that no version of Holmes's reality looks like a happy ending.

Robertson: Well, I know you and I had a lot of thoughts about this movie that we've already discussed, and I'm sure a lot of our viewers would also be interested to see what everybody's talking about. Thanks, Jenny.

Robertson: Over the last few years, several medical organizations have appeared with names that sound a whole lot like other more established physician and research groups. A MedPage Today analysis found that while two groups may have similar names, their views on science can be really different. Cheryl Clark is here to tell us more about this.

Cheryl, can you give us some examples of these newer associations with similar-sounding names to older ones.

Cheryl Clark: Yeah, right, Rachael. You know, we listed seven instances where the names of these new groups sound an awful lot like well-established ones. This is really important because for many of these new entities, when you scroll down and look at their links, you find that they have causes or goals that are diametrically opposed to or fighting against causes that organizations whose names they resemble support.

The biggest, or perhaps most recognizable soundalike example, is the nonprofit Children's Health Defense. That's the one that, last I checked, carries Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s picture at the top of his website, because under his chairmanship in 2018, the name was changed from World Mercury Project to Children's Health Defense. Now, this group has worked to restrict access to childhood vaccines, and it has suggested that vaccines and some environmental contaminants are the underlying cause for autism, despite evidence to the contrary.

But Children's Health Defense sounds a lot like Children's Defense Fund, another nonprofit. Children's Defense Fund is a 53-year-old, well-established organization focused on reducing child hunger and gun violence, and improving health and nutrition, education, and school safety.

Now, both of these organizations want philanthropic donations, but it is interesting that on its website, the Children's Health Defense, that's Kennedy's group, is aware of the potential for confusion. That they want to make sure financial gifts are not inadvertently rerouted. The website says: "Please note, we are often confused with Children's Health Fund or Children's Defense Fund, so be careful not to inadvertently select the wrong recipient."

And by the way, Children's Defense Fund, the long-established group, did tell me that some have confused the two organizations, but they are quick to set the record straight.

Robertson: What are some of the other sound alike groups that have different goals and purposes?

Clark: Right. Well, another interesting one is the American College of Family Medicine (ACFM). Now, it sprouted up in 2023. Sounds official enough, but the ACFM opposes mandatory abortion training and maintains that "abortion is never medically necessary and should not be offered or performed by any health professional." The ACFM sounds an awful lot like the 79-year-old, well-established American Academy of Family Physicians (AAFP), whose membership rolls include 124,000 family doctors. The AAFP has fought back against many Trump administration health policies and activities.

And then there is AAPLOG, or the American Association of Pro-Life Obstetricians and Gynecologists, which in 2013 broke away from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, which has advocated for better maternal health since 1951. AAPLOG has suggested that abortion is linked to depression and substance abuse, and supports the "physician's right of conscience in medical decision making" regarding abortion.

Robertson: There's an obvious question about whether these new organizations purposefully tried to use names that mimic older ones to attract donations. What do you think about that?

Clark: Well, Rachael, I just don't want to touch that one. Although it is an obvious question, groups want to sound official, of course, but whether they were hoping to garner credibility or financial support that way, I have no idea.

Robertson: Well, thank you so much, Cheryl.

Robertson: Some physicians who took the internal medicine board exam on August 13 said that they experienced technical difficulties, and now hundreds of people have been issued indeterminate results on those tests. Kristina Fiore is here to tell us more about this situation.

Kristina, what kind of technical difficulties did they run into?

Kristina Fiore: Yeah, so last month I had a handful of test-takers reach out to me after they received their board exam scores. They all took the test on August 13, and they all described issues when test center staff tried to log them back in after their breaks.

Basically, there are four sections to the test, and you get a break after each one. But sources said that it took an additional 20 to 30 minutes after returning from the breaks to get back into their tests. They all said that they received an email from the American Board of Internal Medicine (ABIM) on the evening of August 13th after taking the test, acknowledging the problem. Now, ABIM said that the program that its testing partner Pearson uses to check people back into the test center after a break malfunctioned, but that email was all that they heard for about two months until the results came back in October.

Robertson: What happened with those results?

Fiore: ABIM told me that 371 test takers received an "indeterminate" result. These are people who did not receive a passing score. An ABIM senior vice president explained that they did this because they're concerned about the... not that they're concerned about the accuracy of their scoring, but because they "cannot know how experiencing a delay logging in to the exam might have affected individual candidates and their performance."

But test-takers I spoke with take issue with that. One of them said they scored unusually low across all subject areas. They questioned whether there could be a frame shift error. This is someone who showed me that they were performing well above average on all of their practice tests. Now, another test-taker said that during her tests, she couldn't select some of the answers and had to click a few times for it to take. So overall, they're concerned that something else went wrong.

Robertson: What has ABIM said to these test takers?

Fiore: When it issued the indeterminate results, it refunded them their $250 exam fee and said that they have the opportunity to retest in the next testing cycle. The problem is that the cycle doesn't start until next August, which means these busy doctors will have to prepare for this test all over again next year, and a lot of them say that that's time they don't really have. ABIM told me that the pass rates on all of the testing days this year were similar and on par with other years, and that they're confident that the scores are accurate. So they are not budging on offering a retake before the next testing cycle.

Robertson: I mean that's a tough situation. Thanks for your reporting here, Kristina.

Robertson: There were more than 500 cases of measles in the past 2 weeks. That's more cases than the U.S. used to see in any given year, excluding this year and last. Pennsylvania is still struggling with 166 cases in the last 2 weeks. The Midwest is also seeing cases rise in states like Wisconsin, Minnesota, Indiana, and Ohio.

As always, check out our interactive measles map, which is linked here, and we update it at the top of each week.

#5793. Nissan Will Pay Toyota RAV4 Owners To Trade Their Car For A New Rogue Hybrid

Nissan's very public struggles are well documented, so it shouldn't come as a surprise that the automaker is taking an aggressive stance with its newest and arguably most important model, the Rogue e-Power Hybrid compact crossover. Compact crossover sales account for a massive share of new car sales each year behind only the full-size pickup segment, with heavyweights like the Honda CR-V, Toyota RAV4, Tesla Model Y, and Nissan Rogue all making the list of the top 10 best-selling cars in the U.S. through Q3 of this year. The Rogue comes in at tenth place on that list, but it turns out Nissan isn't messing around when it comes to improving its ranking, as it's now offering a $1,500 trade-in bonus for anyone who trades a 2021-or-newer Toyota RAV4 for a new Rogue Hybrid.

Our friends at CarsDirect got wind of a dealer bulletin that Nissan sent to its dealers announcing the incentive, which was introduced on November 3 and will run through January 4, 2027.

In order to qualify for the $1,500 trade-in bonus, interested shoppers must have a 2021-or-newer Toyota RAV4 that they trade in when purchasing or leasing a 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid. The deal is transferable to members of the same household, and it can be stacked with Nissan's other current offers. Those other offers include a financing deal of 4.9% APR for 60 months, and a lease deal on the west coast where lessees pay $439 per month for 36 months with $4,959 due at signing and a mileage limit of 10,000 miles per year.

Jalopnik's own Andy Kalmowitz sampled the 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid at the first drive event in Santa Barbara, California, late last month which you can check out here, and he preferred driving the new Rogue Hybrid over the new Toyota RAV4 hybrid.

The 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid features a unique series hybrid drivetrain that operates primarily as an EV. The turbocharged 1.5-liter three-cylinder engine under the hood is solely responsible for charging the Rogue's 1.67-kWh battery, and is not connected to the wheels. The wheels are driven by electric motors mounted on the front and rear axles providing standard all-wheel-drive, and they're capable of scooting the Rogue from 0-to-60 in a quick 6.4 seconds without ever needing to be plugged in. It's rated for 41 mpg in the city, 36 mpg on the highway, and 38 mpg combined which is slightly worse than the RAV4 hybrid, but Andy says the Rogue's interior is a much more comfortable and luxurious space than the RAV4 provides.

#5792. America’s New Shipbuilding Orders Are Expensive Bets on Fossil Freight

South Korea’s Hanwha Group owns the Philadelphia shipyard that has become a centerpiece of Washington’s attempt to rebuild American commercial shipbuilding. Its Hanwha Ocean and Hanwha Systems subsidiaries acquired the US yard in December 2024. The investment creates and sustains American production capacity and jobs while transferring shipbuilding expertise, technology and training from South Korea to US workers. The facility is in America, but its corporate ownership remains South Korean. The company’s published orderbook, however, tells a more complicated story: two liquefied natural gas carriers, four firm orders for oil and chemical tankers, and options for another six tankers. Three LNG-fueled container ships ordered by Matson in 2022 predate the current administration. The newer LNG and tanker orders come from Hanwha’s own shipping affiliates. They can help restart production, but buying ships from another company in the same group does not demonstrate that independent shipowners will pay US construction prices.

The price gap is difficult to dismiss. Kinder Morgan’s January 2026 investor presentation estimates that a new medium-range Jones Act tanker would cost more than $240 million and require a long-term charter above $115,000 per day to justify construction. The existing charter market was around $90,000 per day. Kinder Morgan operates 16 tankers, with its fleet fully utilized, yet the gap between current charter revenue and the cost of a replacement vessel remains substantial. High utilization establishes a need for shipping services; it does not establish a financeable order for a new American-built tanker at today’s prices.

Coastal petroleum shipping also competes with other domestic infrastructure. A 2025 report to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission estimated moving gasoline from Houston to New York Harbor at under 8 cents per gallon by pipeline, about 20 cents by ship, and roughly 35 cents by rail. These illustrative route costs do not cover every destination, and tankers remain essential where pipelines are unavailable. They do show why expensive new tankers cannot count on charter customers accepting whatever price domestic construction requires. Longer term, the International Energy Agency estimates that electric vehicles displaced 1.7 million barrels of oil per day worldwide in 2025 and could displace about 5 million by 2030 under its policy scenarios. That does not mean US tanker demand vanishes, but fleet investment must account for changes in the cargo market over several decades.

LNG export carriers have a more plausible near-term growth market, although their prospects are different from the prospects of LNG-fueled container ships. US gas exports may expand, and LNG tankers will be needed to carry them. The commercial test for a US-built LNG carrier is whether it can win an arm’s-length contract against established Korean, Japanese and Chinese shipyards. Hanwha’s plan to train Philadelphia workers through its Korean shipyards can strengthen US industrial capability, and affiliated orders can provide an initial production run. The central uncertainty is whether independent buyers will still choose these ships once the group’s internal demand and any cargo preference are removed.

A broader domestic vessel market already exists. US-flag Great Lakes freighters carried 71.3 million tons in 2025, much of it iron ore, limestone, cement, coal and other bulk materials. Those cargo flows will change as steelmaking and energy systems evolve, while ferry services, harbour vessels, inland cargo craft and multipurpose ships will still require renewal. Battery-electric and hybrid-electric propulsion offer practical options on routes with manageable energy requirements and reliable charging access. Large, long-distance bulk ships need a more selective technology assessment, rather than an assumption that every vessel can run on batteries.

Recent projects demonstrate what a committed customer can contribute to ship economics. CMA CGM, Nike and Gemadept launched an electric inland barge in Vietnam for a 180-kilometre round trip. Nike agreed to fill 90% of its capacity for eight years, helping justify a vessel reportedly costing about twice as much as its diesel equivalent. A dedicated charging installation and renewable electricity form part of the service. That is a commercially structured freight proposition, with its higher capital cost supported by contracted utilization and expected operating savings.

Electric propulsion does not cure the American shipbuilding cost problem by itself. Washington State’s three new hybrid-electric ferries carry a $714.5 million shipbuilding contract, and the state’s estimate including additional equipment and other program expenses is approximately $1.15 billion. Construction has started; the ferries are not yet in service. The path to a productive shipbuilding industry still runs through standardized designs, modular fabrication, trained workers, repeat orders, reliable delivery and falling labor-hours per vessel. It would be a mistake to treat electrification as a substitute for manufacturing reform.

Hanwha’s South Korean capital and know-how could contribute to that reform by developing US suppliers and production skills that serve several vessel classes. That is a meaningful way to rebuild domestic capability even though the parent company remains foreign-owned. Its progress should ultimately be measured by independent repeat customers, improving construction costs and commercially competitive vessels, rather than affiliated orders or investment announcements. A US maritime strategy anchored to the fossil-fuel cargoes of today risks missing a growing opportunity to build modern domestic vessels for the freight, port and ferry services of tomorrow.

My TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment examines Hanwha’s orders, Kinder Morgan’s tanker economics and the market for repeatable electric and hybrid maritime construction. It follows my earlier analysis of the Jones Act’s shipbuilding capacity gap.

#5791. This Shocking 1997 Ford Ranger EV On Bring A Trailer Is A Splash From The Past

Some may remember the ultra-rare electric Chevy S-10, which was basically an S-10 pickup with GM EV1 running gear. We've seen some versions of the Ranger with an electric shock treatment as well, but not in the cool flareside version known as the Splash. And while it's typically a bad idea to mix electricity and water, this custom EV-converted 1997 Ford Ranger Splash currently for sale on Bring a Trailer is the exception to that rule.

Its bright Canary Yellow paint was an original color for this sporty take on the classic small truck, not a flashy add-on. The original 3.0-liter V6 is gone, replaced with a conversion from Electric Vehicles of America. The Advanced D.C. Motors FB1-4001A motor makes somewhere between 18 and 30 horsepower, a significant downgrade from the original 140 or so from the V6. I know from experience that the V6 wasn't exactly fast, either, so hopefully the instant electric torque makes up for some of the lost power.

The retention of the original five-speed manual transmission is also a nice touch. We've seen this before in EV swaps into vehicles not intended for EV swaps as an easy way to connect the electric motor to the original driveline. According to the instructions taped to the dashboard, there is no clutch, so you just start it in a low gear, then shift to whatever gear best matches your speed. The factory cupholders are still there (which I know from experience will still let your drinks tip over when going around corners at even a moderate speed), and there are three gauges for battery volts (power usage), amps (how much power is left), and a level of charge gauge. There's also a warning light for a hot motor and and on/off switch for the 1,500-watt electric heater, since there's no internal combustion engine to generate heat anymore.

Unlike some modern project EVs, this Ranger followed a simpler approach, which is easier to install and maintain. Rather than a slick Tesla battery pack, it uses a bank of 20 Trojan six-volt batteries, wired in series to produce the 120 volts the motor and Curtis controller need to run the truck. Some of the batteries live in a box between the frame rails, some in the bed like a Cybertruck, and a few under the hood. That's also where the charger lives, so you have to pop the hood to plug it into a standard household outlet. There's no fast charging for this Ranger.

You won't be going very far between charges, either. Electric Vehicles of America estimates the range to be somewhere between 38 and 81 miles, with an average of 53. That's on new batteries, which these are not. EVs have become much more practical in recent years, but the technology in this Ranger is relatively old and crude, so it's pretty much limited to short runs around town between long charging cycles.

If you can live with these limitations, this is actually a great project EV. It's simple enough to be fairly reliable. You can likely maintain it and fix it yourself, and all of the documentation you need is included. It's not perfect, with a torn headliner and some dents and dings around the body, but it's still in good shape for a 1997 Ranger, and easy to fix. It has no reserve and at the time of writing, it has a high bid of $300. I'm sure that will change, but hopefully it will stay less expensive than a Slate truck. Plus, this truck has something no Slate, Cybertruck, or Rivian has: It's a Ford f'in Ranger.

#5790. As Jackery Inventory Sells Out, Are Portable Batteries Set To Take Off?

I recently wrote reviews of the new Jackery HomePower 1000 Plus v2 and Explorer 100D. A few days later, a connection with Jackery messaged me that their Black Friday/Cyber Monday products had largely sold out. Just three days after launching on November 1. This includes 1000, 2000, 3600 and 5000 portable power and solar generator models. Additional models have sold out since then or will likely sell out soon. The recently launched Explorer 100D is still available in limited quantities at Walmart and Costco.

While Jackery will still take orders for Black Friday/Cyber Monday sales, most models currently listed for purchase will be on a preorder basis. Customers should check estimated delivery dates. Some restocking is expected in late November, although broader inventory availability may not recover until early next year.

While much of America was recovering from Halloween and election victory parties, portable batteries were selling out. This wasn’t the result of limited supply, but rather a massive, unanticipated increase in demand.

Between October 19th  and 26th, Jackery retail sales increased 755% at Costco, 106% at Walmart, 297% at The Home Depot and 442% at Lowes. For added perspective, at Costco alone, sales increased from 2379 to 20,343 over that one week.

Jackery is looking into what’s behind the massive increase in demand. Clearly, there have been climate-related disasters over the past year, including hurricanes and wildfires. Jackery’s collaboration with the Red Cross helps illustrate the benefits of portable power in emergency response. However, that only partially explains the growth. A related potential explanation is the growing push for household preparedness.  There are reports of at least 17 countries encouraging people to keep three to seven days of food, water and other essentials. Winter storm season, grid strain and rising energy costs could be stoking fears of potential power outages. The US FORTRESS America initiative has also added an emphasis on resilience. Together, these signals may be pushing “preparedness” beyond food and water to include power.

Preparedness is gaining emphasis with power becoming an increasingly important part of being prepared. The fear of “what if” can be a powerful motivator. Having backup power can keep the air handlers working for people’s furnaces. People on well water can keep the pumps running. Backup power can keep refrigerators full of food from spoiling.

Overall, Jackery is the global leader in solar generator sales volume and was named the “World’s No.1 Solar Generator Brand” by Frost & Sullivan. With over 15 years of experience and extensive safety protocols, the brand is well established. For the purchase of a product that manages risks, having a trusted brand is clearly valuable.

Although there has not been a detailed study of the consumer motivations, preparedness is likely a major motivator. However, versatile portable power stations have additional benefits. I keep finding new ways to use the HomePower 1000 Plus V2. And new possible benefits keep opening up.

Beyond providing emergency power, I can take power with me. I can set up an office remotely. I can run and recharge tools away from an outlet. I can power a radiant heater for a few hours while sitting outdoors. I can power an air conditioner for hours or run a fan all day. I can make coffee and cook food. In many ways, the batteries can replace functions once covered not just by a generator, but also a campfire or grill.

While using the battery, I also became more aware of my electricity usage. Seeing how quickly different appliances deplete the battery makes me realize where my utility bill is really going. Some things use less electricity than I anticipated, and some use far more. That awareness helps me to reduce my overall consumption.

And the UPS function can also save delicate equipment, as well as any work on computers and other machinery during a power disruption. I personally would not run a large print on my 3D printer without the backup battery. Providing stable power can extend the lifespan of many expensive devices.

The ability to integrate solar panels provides an additional level of preparedness, allowing the battery to be recharged by the sun when grid power is not available. However, solar can also charge the battery for daily use. While this may not yet be able to feed into the grid without additional equipment, people can reasonably use solar power fed into the battery to replace grid power at the point of use. When the regulations are figured out, balcony solar could expand the possibilities. All this can reduce people’s energy costs.

The battery can provide power when they need it, rather than just when the sun is shining. And when connected to the grid with a time of use (TOU) plan, it can charge when electricity is inexpensive and provide power when it is expensive. The savings from this alone could pay for the battery and start saving people money on their utility bills. And the grid becomes more stable in the process.

If the current battery capacity is not enough, Jackery makes expandible batteries to add more capacity.

In addition, the portable, scalable batteries can form the foundation of a whole home system. With greater utility communication, the added capacity could open up new possibilities for users to benefit while they help stabilize the grid. And they still benefit from the backup power. In addition, after seeing the capabilities, some people may even be inspired to look into going off-grid.

Of course, Jackery is likely not the only company seeing a surge in sales. I hope consumer demand and adoption is rising across the board. With a low barrier to entry and the ability to provide a level of preparedness, sales of portable batteries are likely to continue to grow.

Jackery is actively focused on removing the barriers to entry. Then the benefits of battery backup and portable power can be realized by more people. As more people see the benefits of portable expandable batteries, more people will want them. As more battery capacity is deployed, more applications can become viable. That not only has the ability to make homes more resilient, but also to build a more resilient grid. With the ability to shift consumption through distributed storage, more renewable energy can be utilized.

People who may have bought originally for preparedness will start to realize the broader benefits of their purchase. When people benefit from something, they will tend to rationalize it. This typically works better to change perspectives than trying to start with a rational argument. When people feel the relief of having backup power available for “what if,” they can then expand upon that with greater feelings of independence. Once they personally benefit from the storage that enables greater renewable adoption, they may increase their support for renewable energy. By addressing fears of “what if,” people may open themselves to thinking about “what’s possible.”

Of course, this might just be a temporary sales blip. But it could also be the start of a rapid expansion in home battery use. That could open up a wide range of new possibilities.

#5789. 'ER' and 'The Pitt' Similar Enough for Lawsuit to Move Forward, Appeals Court Says

— The lawsuit was filed 2 years ago by the "ER" creator's wife and estate

A California appeals court has found that "ER" and "The Pitt" have enough similarity that a lawsuit brought by the widow and estate of "ER" creator Michael Crichton alleging "The Pitt" is an unauthorized reboot can move forward.

A three-judge panel from California's 2nd District Court of Appeal ruled unanimously on Wednesday that the trial court judge was correct to reject a motion to throw out the case from "The Pitt" production company Warner Bros. Television, which also produced "ER." But the judges dismissed Noah Wyle -- the star of both shows and a producer on "The Pitt" -- as a defendant along with two other producers who worked on both series.

The lawsuit is a clash between the makers of multiple Emmy-winning TV series that were each among the most important and acclaimed shows of their eras.

Crichton, the author of "Jurassic Park" and many other novels that became hit movies and TV shows, wrote the pilot script for "ER," the NBC show about a Chicago emergency room that redefined the medical drama genre and drew tens of millions of weekly viewers in its run from 1994 to 2009.

The lawsuit brought by Sherri Crichton was filed 2 years ago, before a single episode of "The Pitt" had aired. The HBO Max series that shows a real-time day in the life of a Pittsburgh emergency department has since become perhaps the most lauded series in television, winning two Emmys for best drama for its first two seasons and two best actor Emmys for Wyle.

Along with more technical legal issues, the judges had to decide whether the shows had at least the minimal similarity that would give the lawsuit enough merit to move forward. Their decision applies only to this early legal challenge and they did not rule on whether the plaintiffs had proved that "The Pitt" is derivative of "ER."

The court agreed with the plaintiff that "both shows provide commentaries on the healthcare system; they focus specifically on the emergency room and the difficult conditions under which the medical staff operates. Both shows take place, with little exception, in the emergency room, as opposed to other medical shows which track patients as they move out of the emergency room, or indeed never enter it."

The opinion also said that both feature "very fast pacing, and reactions to multiple overlapping crises. The fast-paced dialogue is (to a layperson) frequently incomprehensible shorthand and jargon, lending an air of immediacy and accuracy."

Warner Bros. Television said in a statement that "WBTV continues to maintain that 'The Pitt' is an entirely original series and that the claims against it are without merit. Nothing in the Court of Appeal's decision establishes otherwise, and WBTV looks forward to defending its position as the case proceeds."

The defendants argued in legal filings that the shows have "generic similarities" that would exist in "any dramatic story" that features "overworked doctors and staff."

The panel also unanimously dismissed as defendants Wyle; John Wells, who created "The Pitt" and worked on "ER"; and R. Scott Gemmill, a "Pitt" executive producer who also worked on both shows. The judges found there was no evidence the three men knew the provisions of the Crichton contract that the lawsuit alleges they interfered with.

Sherri Crichton's lawsuit alleges "The Pitt" is a rebranded version of an unauthorized "ER" reboot that she had rejected.

Her husband had secured a coveted "frozen rights" provision in his contract for the series, prohibiting Warner Bros. from proceeding with any sequels, remakes, spinoffs, or other productions derived from "ER" without Crichton's consent, or his estate's consent after his death from cancer in 2008.

After the production company could not reach an agreement with Sherri Crichton over a proposed "ER" reboot, the TV studio proceeded to develop and produce a series based on the same premise without permission, the lawsuit alleges.

There’s a solid chance these companies would no longer exist today without that early support. Democrats in California and in the US government were also critical to consumer support for electric vehicles, air pollution standards for electric vehicles, and carbon credit markets that have led to billions of dollars of revenue for Tesla. Tesla would most certainly not have been able to rise and evolve as it did without all of that support — and, again, it’s questionable whether the company would have ever gotten profitable and been alive today if it didn’t have that strong support from Democrats. Republicans in power have not been willing to support EVs, put stronger pollution limits on gasmobiles, or require higher levels of fuel economy from automakers. Every time they have all the power of the US government, they go the other direction on these things.

Of course, we know that Elon Musk shifted to the right politically (to the far, far right) after a few things happened. Those key things were as follows:

Overall, historically, Democrats have been the ones who have pushed strong policies in support of the clean technologies Tesla develops and sells. However, because of the above (as well as a ton of seeming corruption and anti-democratic, oligarchic influence), Musk has been one of the top funders and campaigners for the Republican Party in recent elections. In this most recent midterm election, he was the single largest individual donor in the country, providing at least $447 million to try to get Republicans elected — completely unsuccessfully (well, like 99.99% unsuccessfully or something like that).

If Elon Musk had continued on his previous rather nonpartisan or bipartisan tendencies, who knows what this election would have meant for Tesla (and SpaceX). However, now that he has become the #1 Republican donor in the United States, and heavily stacked his social media platform in support of Republicans, one has to wonder how Democrats in control of Congress — and perhaps later on the presidency — will respond to the countless attacks Musk has waged against them. It’s logical to assume there will be repercussions. Perhaps they won’t target him unfairly, but they may well choose to investigate and seek punishments for illegal activity, provable corruption, and undemocratic behavior. Instead of this gigantic blue wave being something we could expect to help Tesla, everyone is now wondering if Tesla is going to face some serious consequences.

As a result, reportedly, Tesla and SpaceX lost $420 billion (yes, billion) in market cap following the election — ironically. Perhaps that value has changed now, but how fitting is it that this is the punishment the market is delivering for Elon Musk being so massively wrong politically. For now.

#5787. Honda Dealer Sued For 'Obnoxious' AI Robocalls To A Guy Who Didn't Want To Sell Them His Car

You get them. I get them. We all get them. AI robocalls are a nightmare scourge on society that are driving everybody to the brink of their sanity. Usually, they're from some sort of money-lending organization. Still, one Massachusetts man says he keeps receiving pre-recorded phone calls from Cambridge Honda asking him whether he was interested in selling them his car. Now, he's seeking class-action status against the dealership, alleging that it violated the Telephone Consumer Protection Act.

Plaintiff Jonathan Kamens has never been a customer at Cambridge Honda, and his cell phone number is on the National Do Not Call Registry, according to Automotive News. The complaint alleges that an AI-generated caller with a "robotic and artificial voice" addresses Kamens by the wrong name, "Timothy," and then says, "Roger from Cambridge Honda. Reaching out because you're one of our customers, and your car happens to be on a list of models we are looking to buy. If you're open to an instant cash offer on your car, give me a call at (351) 300-0683. Thanks." Kamens added that he received subsequent texts from "Roger" inviting him to sell his vehicle — something he really has no interest in doing.

In an effort to get answers, Kamens called the number back. A voice at the other end answered, but when he started the conversation asking if the person was real or not, it said it was AI, according to AutoNews, which received the same automated response when it called the number.

"Moreover, the call injured [Kamens] because it was frustrating, obnoxious, annoying and a nuisance and disturbed [his] solitude," it said.

While this is true, it's also funny to think about suing someone because they took away from your screen time. I mean, I would, but you get what I'm saying.

The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, asked for certification of the class, damages and an order prohibiting Cambridge Honda from "making calls, except for emergency purposes, to any cellular telephone numbers using an artificial or prerecorded voice in the future." The Honda dealer, for its part, has remained quiet. A lawyer representing the store said she wasn't authorized to discuss the case.

It's not clear how many times Kamens was contacted by the dealer or how many people in total were impacted, but if they're going for a class action, my gut tells me it's not "a few."

#5786. Booze, Tobacco Together in Pregnancy May Worsen Baby's Facial Abnormalities

— Smaller face size, reduced growth, and dysmorphism worse with combined exposure, study shows

Prenatal exposure to both alcohol and tobacco smoke impacted the baby's facial development more than either alone, a longitudinal study from South Africa showed.

Three-dimensional facial scans at 1 month and 1 year of age showed the greatest differences in facial shape, size, and growth with co-exposure from early pregnancy compared with none or single-substance exposure, Michael Suttie, PhD, of the University of Oxford in England, and colleagues reported in Pediatrics.

For girls, tobacco plus alcohol exposure was associated with greater reductions in facial growth and measurements around the eyes. Craniofacial growth didn't catch up by age 1 for girls exposed continuously to both substances in utero. For boys, dual prenatal exposure was linked to reduced nasal growth, resulting in smaller noses at 1 year.

"Findings highlight tobacco's potentiating effect on alcohol-related craniofacial harm," the researchers wrote. "These findings highlight the importance of interventions targeting alcohol and smoking cessation during pregnancy to reduce teratogenic risk."

An estimated 5.4% of U.S. women smoke during pregnancy, which carries known risk of craniofacial developmental issues for the baby, including craniosynostosis and orofacial clefts. Some 9.8% of pregnant women globally consume alcohol, which can lead to the baby having facial characteristics such as nasal shortening, midline differences, midfacial hypoplasia, ocular differences, and mandibular anomalies aside from some of the most identifiable signs of fetal alcohol syndrome: a smooth philtrum above a short upper lip and shortened width from the inner to outer corner of the eye.

"Both teratogens are known to disrupt neural crest cell migration, survival, and differentiation, processes essential for the formation of midline facial structures, ocular features, and nasal morphology," the researchers noted. "Nicotine exposure potentially compounds this disruption [by alcohol] through oxidative stress, hypoxia, and nicotine-induced vasoconstriction, which may impair oxygen and nutrient delivery during critical periods of facial morphogenesis."

To look for evidence that the impact of these substances might be additive, Suttie's group examined the Safe Passage Study, a prospective cohort of more than 7,000 pregnancies in low socioeconomic communities in Cape Town, South Africa, which has one of the world's highest rates of alcohol use in pregnancy. The cohort largely comprised women of mixed ancestry, known as South African Colored.

Of the more than 7,000 participants in the study, the analysis homed in on the subset of 634 participants who had 3D facial imaging of their infants at age 1 month and 1 year and antenatal substance exposure data. Exclusion criteria included illicit drug use by the mother (including marijuana) and genetic diagnoses in infants.

Alcohol and smoking exposures had been assessed via interview at each prenatal visit, with frequency and quantity both captured. Continuous exposure was defined as exposure in the first trimester and any subsequent trimester. There were 152 infants categorized as without exposure, 48 with continuous alcohol-only exposure, 149 with continuous smoking-only exposure, 150 with continuous co-exposure, and 135 with continuous smoking and any alcohol use.

Continuous prenatal co-exposure to smoking and alcohol was associated with reduced facial size compared with both controls and single-exposure groups (P<0.05), driven by differences among girls. The single-exposure groups showed no differences compared with controls.

"Our findings of sex-specific dysmorphism are consistent with prior work suggesting differential vulnerability to prenatal alcohol exposure by sex," Suttie and colleagues noted.

Continuous co-exposure was associated with greater facial dysmorphism overall, with the biggest difference at 1 month (P<0.001) but still significant at 1 year (P<0.05). Consistent midline displacement was seen with co-exposure at both time points. More outward lateral movement of the inner canthi of the eye was also seen with co-exposure at both time points (P<0.05).

Limitations included the need to scan infants while sleeping, potential modification by maternal nutritional deficiencies, and unknown generalizability to populations with different genetic profiles.

"Our results contribute to a growing body of evidence on the harms of co-exposures, and we encourage clinicians and healthcare authorities to emphasize the potential harm of concurrent smoking and alcohol use during pregnancy," the researchers concluded.

#5785. Kawasaki Z1000, Yamaha FZ6 Quad, Subaru Sambar: The Dopest Cars I Found For Sale Online

Happy whatever day it is, friends. It's been a ride this past week — things have been weird, and almost exclusively in good ways. You remember good things, right? Turns out, those can still happen! This whole time, while things have been weird and bad, they could have been weird and good instead. What a concept!

Today, in honor of that, we're looking at some fascinating listings from across Facebook Marketplace. Not just cool cars or good deals, but trying to find the specifically weird and interesting — things you wouldn't necessarily expect, but are happy to see. We've got suspiciously cheap bikes, kei trucks, even a completely banal and unremarkable commuter car from 2013. What's less expected around these parts than that? So come in, take a load off, and let's walk hand in hand through the new world we've wrought. Well, its car listings at least. Welcome, my friends, to this week's Dopest Cars.

Did you know Kawasaki naked literbikes cost under seven grand used? I had no idea, but this Z1000 for $6,999 feels like a genuinely great price. This isn't some clapped-out Hayabusa for cheap, it's a modern bike that seems to be in good condition, one that's actually enjoyable to use as a daily rider. Want to go a million miles per hour on the cheap, without having a bike that's a pain to lug through your commute? The Z1000 awaits.

I will say, for those eyeing this bike, that you should probably budget for some extra expenses. It looks like whatever tail tidy this Z has is one that combines the rear turn signals into the brake light, which is difficult for drivers to see — take it from someone who's put low-profile blinkers on a bike before, I felt safer with lights on stalks. If I were to buy this, I'd want to add some properly visible turn signals back to the rear end.

I've long been browsing the livable vehicle market, but my recent renewed seriousness and urgency in shopping for vans and campers has had an odd side effect: I've gotten extremely brown-beige-RV-pilled. I don't know how or why it happened, but suddenly I'm looking at these deeply '80s-looking campers and thinking about how much I want one. I don't think I could stand to live in a house that looked as dated as this Econoline camper, but put it on wheels and suddenly I'm sold.

I do wonder, in a camper this old, how much of a risk of mold there is. After all, these things live outside, and seals are known to fail. I worry about mold in New York apartments all the same, and least this would let me own a dwelling that I could keep around if the economy tanks and I get booted from my apartment. That's been on my mind recently, for no particular reason.

I'm not much of a drag girlie, in either automotive or nightlife terms, but this RX-8 dragster deserves special consideration. First off, it's not yet another V8 build — this one has a three-rotor engine, about which the seller says absolutely nothing else. That's already pretty unique within the drag racing world, but then you come to the body of this car. It's not a dedicated top fuel look, it's not a  better-looking RX-7, it's for some reason an RX-8. I don't get it, but I do love it.

The RX-8 is probably the worst looking of Mazda's RX line (though it's still pretty good relative to any car not built by Mazda), and the structure beneath the body appears to be a totally custom tube chassis. There's no real reason to make the body look like this other than someone's enthusiasm for the model. It does get bonus points for having Han's paint job, though.

At some point in this Barracuda's life, someone wanted to take it racing. That time was long enough ago that the car no longer turns over, and judging from the construction of the half-rollcage and the design of the steering wheel we're looking at a time even before that last tank of now-skunked fuel was put in the car. Since then, some rust has bubbled up, and the tires have dry rotted away.

The car, though, still deserves that chance at being truly run ragged on track. If you can fix it up to a usable state, grind back the rust and clear out the fuel system, you'll have a classic muscle car with updated engine electronics and at least some rudimentary chassis bracing — I'm not sure how much that half cage helps the body's stiffness, but it probably doesn't hurt in the corners. Can you imagine rolling up to your local HPDE in this?

The seller lists this as an R6 quad in the ad title, but the description is more accurate: The quad is actually built around a Yamaha FZ6, the more upright cousin to the R6. I see why the seller went for the better-known bike in the listing headline, but the FZ6 is the better bike to start with for something like this. Sure, you're going to mess with the ergonomics anyway, but I'd rather start with the more comfortable bike and build out from there.

Is this quad good? I haven't ridden it to know for sure, but I'm willing to bet that it's not. The R6 engine shared by the FZ6 isn't exactly known for its low-end torque, and an off-road setup like this — an ATV on all-terrain tires — probably isn't going to see much time screaming at redline on the highway. Whether the quad is fun, though, is another question entirely. I love it when something's a little bit dumb.

Today on "Amber begs sellers to take even one decent photo of the items they're selling," I had to combine two separate shots of this Chevy Spark to get one halfway usable photo for this section. It was worth it, though, because Jalop Slack was actually fondly reminiscing about the Spark just the other day. It, too, is a car that's genuinely bad yet still kind of endearing.

I still remember the first time I drove a Spark, long before I worked here. It was bright green with a manual transmission, and upon getting in I wiggled the shifter to ensure it was in neutral, started the car, and took my foot off the clutch. It stalled. It had been in first the whole time, but the shifter had as much play in gear as my Subaru at the time had in neutral. Deeply bad car. I'm genuinely kind of considering buying this one.

Here's a truly unusual one. Not the Lada, we've had a few of those grace this hallowed column, but its history: The seller claims this is a one-owner Lada. Now, take a walk with me, because that's going to mean this car has a truly interesting story. The plate suggests this is registered, which means it's been properly imported and had all its paperwork done. Of course, given the 25-year law, it couldn't have come into the country before 2011. If this truly is a one-owner car, that means someone owned it in Russia or a former Soviet state before emigrating to the United States.

This car would have, under its current ownership, seen the fall of the Berlin wall. Its owner would have driven it through the dissolution of the Soviet Union, and into the modern establishment of whichever Iron Curtain nation it was originally sold in. Then, it and its owner would have both moved here, and watched our modern political environment. Maybe this Lada is cursed, actually.

If you're looking to get into motorcycling, now's the time. This seller is asking $2,500 for this Rebel 300 — one of the all-time great first bikes — and they've been asking that for seven weeks now. They don't want to store this all winter, a bike they're already looking to get rid of so they can upgrade. They want the thing gone, and I'm willing to bet that "No low ball" line in the ad gets less and less strict with each passing day. When the first snow falls, will this seller still want to have this bike taking up space? No.

You could likely get this bike for a song right now, and you'd end up with one of the best beginner bikes ever made. There's a reason these are beloved by MSF courses — this one could well be a former MSF bike, given its aftermarket replacements for the mirrors that instructors would've removed. If you have space to throw a bike through the winter (or warm enough gear to ride through the cold), you can get a screaming deal on a first motorcycle right here.

Back in the day, I had a friend with a Fiat 500 Abarth much like this one. Theirs was wrapped purple and tuned, with aftermarket intake piping powdercoated in Tiffany Blue, but beyond that it was just like this. That little Fiat was one of the most fun cars I ever got to ride in, and I think you should try one out for yourself.

Stock 500 Abarths are fun, but a tune really wakes them up. This wide-eyed little gummy candy of a car suddenly becomes a small rocket bound for low earth orbit, and you're left to do nothing but hang on and laugh manically until you get back to the Starbucks parking lot that hosts your car meet. Then, with the engine up to temperature, you can stuff the back half of your Chipotle burrito into the intake piping to reheat it. What other car has a built-in microwave for your leftovers?

Back in the day, there was a rule on Dopest: If I saw a kei car, it went in the column. That's gone by the wayside as more and more kei cars have showed up on Marketplace, with ground ceded to my rules against double-dipping on automakers, but this Sambar deserved the honor once so freely doled out to its brethren — if anything, an honor made all the more meaningful by its newfound rarity.

These kei cars technically aren't legal to register in New York State, but some folks seem to get them through the system. This one avoids the rules by being located in Jersey, but it deserves to be able to come to the greatest city in the world. I deserve to be able to drive one of these to the crag, is what I'm saying. If I can't, though, you should do so in my stead.

#5784. Alas, Poor Cybertruck, We Hardly Knew Thee

If you felt a ripple in the space-time continuum yesterday, yes, the rumors are true. All too sadly true. The Tesla Cybertruck EV, introduced to motorists in 2019 with great fanfare and a sales goal of up to 250,000 units per year, is slated to cross the rainbow bridge into the dustbine of automotive history sometime next year. Not to worry, Tesla fans. Rumor has it that Tesla’s Cybercab robotaxi will pick up where the Cybertruck left off — oh, wait. Hold, please…

Tesla is notoriously shy about releasing sales figures, but there are ways to reach an approximation. Earlier this year CleanTechnica calculated that the Cybertruck barely scraped by 2025 with just 17,012 units delivered. Even so, just one year earlier Tesla CEO Elon Musk was still pitching the 250,000 Cybertrucks-per-year goal.

Even though it is soon to be gone, the Cybertruck will never be forgotten. Much in the same way as the Edsel, “Cybertruck” will linger on as shorthand for a fabulously hyped product without an audience.

The Cybertruck was promised as a full sized, five-seat electric pickup truck with ample storage room. Tesla delivered on the zero emission angle, of course, and the five seats, too. However, the automaker failed to deliver on pickup truckyness in any substantive way (see entire CleanTechnica archive here).

So…don’t let the door hit you on the way out. Multiple electric pickup trucks are taking up the space left by the Cybertruck, including the forthcoming Ford Fathom alongside offerings from Rivian, Slate Auto, and other automakers.

Elon Musk himself announced the untimely death of the Cybertruck in a post on his social media site X earlier today.

“Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production,” Musk stated somewhat blandly, perhaps expecting his audience to appreciate the good news about “increased Cybercab production.”

If so, Musk was probably disappointed to hear from X users like Ben McCombe, who skipped over the implication that the Cybercap would occupy more space in the Tesla Gigafactory in Austin, Texas. Instead, he zeroed in on the Cybertruck in a particularly pithy comment:

“Installed tooling to build 125k Cybertrucks a year.

“Made just $100m in gross profits from sales.

Tesla’s stock tanked on November 3 and the following two days, after Democratic candidates dominated the all-important mid-term elections in both Houses of Congress, and in statehouses across the country including Tesla’s home state, Texas. The power shift all but guarantees a more vigorous application of federal and state regulations governing Tesla’s products and operations.

Still, the automaker scored a partial recovery just a few days later. Tesla stock was swinging upwards as of mid-day on November 6, with Musk’s Cybercab announcement possibly factored into the partial recovery. However, those incoming lawmakers are going to be taking a close look at the Cybercab, and so far the picture is not pretty.

One sign of trouble emerged on September 3, when Musk failed to appear at a long-anticipated Cybercab launch event in Texas. The very next day, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration went out of its way to let everyone know that it is investigating Tesla’s self-certification for the Cybercab under the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act.

“The US Department of Transportation’s National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) today announced that it has opened an Audit Query (AQ) to investigate Tesla’s certification that its new Cybercab meets all applicable Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS),” NHTSA announced on September 4.

NHTSA initially gave Tesla until September 30 to respond to a list of 21 questions about the Cybercab self-certification, then extended the deadline to October 30.

Anyone eager to learn how automakers go about self-certifying new models under the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act will be sorely disappointed, unless they are privileged to read the documents Tesla finally submitted. “The tricky part is that in its public response, Tesla offered one whole sentence. ‘The entirety of this file is confidential business information,'” Carscoops reported earlier today.

So close and yet so far. While the Cybercab investigation is still bubbling away on the backburner, Tesla has also set itself up for a whole ‘nother round of investigations related to its newly unveiled “flying car,” part of a suite of high-end sports cars modeled after the original Tesla Roadster.

The Roadster reboot was slightly clouded by the release of a new documentary on Elon Musk’s rise to both automotive and political power, but just slightly. The automotive press went nuts over the spectacle of the new Tesla Roadster Rocket going airborne for a few seconds, then safely landing on all four tires with an assist from SpaceX-designed thrusters.

Whether or not that actually counts as a flight or just a thruster-enhanced jump, the Federal Aviation Administration has already stated that the Rocket does not meet its definition of an aircraft.

As of for the question of whether or not the vehicle can be used on public roads, that’s something for the NTHSA to weigh in on. On Tesla’s part, though, the automaker has reportedly stated that the Rocket is not designed for use on public roads. That seems to cut NTHSA out of the picture, though some industry observers have suggested that the agency could adopt a framework that encompasses vehicles with thrusters.

Musk himself has suggested that anyone who purchases the thruster-equipped Roadster can make it fly on a purpose-built tack on Tesla (or perhaps SpaceX) property, presumably in Texas.

The land use issue opens up a whole ‘nother can of worms regarding Musk’s operations in Texas. If anything, the offer of an off-road Rocket track seems could to let Tesla off the hook for the actions of any rambunctious Rocket driver who insists on trialing the car on public roads.

For the record, “Musk” the movie opened initially in Los Angeles and New York City on October 9. A wide release on hundreds of screens was scheduled for October 16, but the film’s distributor, Bleecker Street,” abruptly pulled back on the plan under new ownership. On October 27, representatives for the film contacted CleanTechnica to clarify that the “Musk” documentary was still showing on scores of screens around the country even after the dial-down. Either way, if you missed it in theaters, you can catch the whole thing — including the Cybertruck debacle and so much more — streaming as of today, November 6, on Amazon Prime Video, iTunes, and YouTube along with cable services.

#5782. What Is a Great Google Quality Real Estate Score: A Comprehensive Guide

Navigating the world of Google Ads can be challenging, especially in an industry as competitive as real estate. One term you've probably heard in relation to Google Ads is "Quality Score." This score is crucial to how your ads perform and how much they cost. But what does it mean for realtors, and what constitutes a great Google Quality Real Estate Score? Let's dive in.

Google Ads Quality Score is essentially a measurement of the quality and relevance of both your keywords and PPC ads. It is a dynamic metric, assigned on a scale of 1 to 10, with 10 being the best possible score. It is used by Google to determine your cost per click (CPC) and your ad rank in the ad auction process.

Quality Score is calculated based on three primary components: click-through rate (CTR), ad relevance, and landing page experience.

For any industry, including real estate, a good Quality Score is generally around 7 or above. However, in the competitive world of real estate, striving for an even higher Quality Score could give you an advantage. So, for realtors, a great Quality Score might be considered 8 or above.

That said, keep in mind that a high-Quality Score is not an end in itself. It's a sign that your ads are relevant, and your landing pages provide a good user experience, but it's still just one factor in the overall success of your Google Ads campaigns.

A high-Quality Score is beneficial for several reasons:

Improving your Quality Score is all about relevance and user experience. Here are some strategies:

A high Google Ads Quality Score can be a strong asset for realtors. It not only helps you rank higher and pay less for clicks but also ensures your ads are shown to the most relevant audiences. However, remember that Quality Score is just one piece of the puzzle. You should also consider other factors like your bidding strategy and overall account performance to create a successful Google Ads campaign.

Healthcare payment software maker Waystar again outperformed analysts’ estimates in the third quarter as the company builds out new artificial intelligence capabilities and drives growth by adding new customers and selling more of its platform to existing clients.

Waystar brought in $325.6 million in Q3 revenue, up 21% from the same period a year ago, according to its Q3 financial results published Monday afternoon. It beat Wall Street analysts’ estimates by 0.46%.

During Q3, the company reported $181 million in subscription revenue, up 34%, while provider revenue grew 28% to reach $243 million. Patient revenue came in at $82 million, up 5% year-over-year, and volume-based revenue grew 8% to $143 million.

Waystar ended the quarter with 1,488 clients generating more than $100,000 of trailing 12-month revenue, up 14% year-over-year. Year-to-date bookings grew 25% year-over-year.

Waystar reported net income of $31 million and GAAP net income per share of 16 cents. It also reported adjusted EBITDA of $139.3 million and non-GAAP earnings per share of 44 cents.

Waystar provides healthcare payment and revenue cycle management tools to 30,000 clients, representing over 1.5 million distinct providers. Its platform processes over 8.5 billion healthcare payment transactions annually, representing more than $3 trillion in gross claims, according to CEO Matt Hawkins. Waystar says its clinical intelligence spans approximately one-third of U.S. hospital discharges. In 2026, Waystar added more than 100 direct connections to health plans, supporting nearly 50 million transactions annually, executives said.

Hawkins told investors and analysts during the Q3 earnings call that the quarter “reflects strong progress,” on three strategic priorities of “driving broader adoption of the Waystar platform, extending our reach through partners and integrations, and advancing AI and innovation.”

“Our near-term roadmap includes more than 20 planned AI capabilities, accelerating the autonomous revenue cycle vision to reduce manual work, automate increasingly complex tasks and improve financial and operational outcomes for our clients,” Hawkins said.

Waystar is focused on using AI to reshape the RCM process with a vision of building an "autonomous revenue cycle" that can reduce manual work, automate increasingly complex tasks and improve financial and operational outcomes for healthcare organizations, executives said.

In Q3, Waystar launched an autonomous claim resubmission capability that interprets payer responses, applies payer-specific intelligence to determine the next action and autonomously resubmits eligible rejected claims with minimal human intervention, Hawkins said.

"Based on early adopter results and the initial claim types supported, we estimate this capability could autonomously resubmit up to $5 billion in previously rejected claims annually with the potential to eliminate more than 400,000 hours of manual work each year," he said.

The company is also targeting mid-cycle processes. "We're combining Waystar's financial data, payer intelligence, workflows and connectivity with Iodine's clinical intelligence to bring greater automation earlier in the revenue cycle," Hawkins noted.

The company acquired AI-driven RCM company Iodine Software a year ago to add its clinical intelligence capabilities to Waystar's software. Iodine bookings exceeded management's year-to-date plan by 74% in Q3, Hawkins said. Iodine's CDI and pre-bill anomaly detection products generated nearly $30 million in bookings through Q3, including about $15 million during the quarter, and have a combined pipeline exceeding $100 million.

The company is winning bigger, broader deals in the healthcare market, Hawkins asserted. Large health care organizations increasingly look to Waystar to support more of the revenue cycle through a single connected platform, he said on the call. "Within our large client cohort, which we define as clients generating more than $100,000 in LTM revenue, the average client now uses approximately five Waystar product modules. With over 30 modules across six product families, we see significant opportunity to continue driving broader platform adoption within these relationships," he said.

Hawkins added that the company “secured the largest new client win in Waystar’s history” during Q3.

“In a competitive process, a major East Coast health system representing approximately $7 billion in annual net patient revenue selected Waystar's full platform across patient access, mid-cycle, and back-end revenue cycle operations,” he said. “The organization plans to replace more than 20 separate vendors with Waystar as it simplifies its technology infrastructure and streamlines operations.”

Moreover, Hawkins said the company is expanding its reach with “strategic channel relationships,” with an emphasis on the ambulatory market—noting an expanded partnership with a leading physical therapy practice management system that expands Waystar’s reach to “nearly 4,000 providers across more than 2,500 sites, representing approximately 17 million claims annually.”

“Decisions like these reflect the trust we've built with channel partners, the breadth of our platform, and our ability to deliver real ROI,” Hawkins said.

Alpana Wegner, who took over as Waystar’s chief financial officer in August, said that large client relationships “now represent approximately 75% of revenue,” adding the company is seeing momentum across growth in number of clients, strong bookings and implementation backlog expansion.

But larger, broader platform implementations have longer revenue conversion times, which can extend to 12 to 18 months, Wegner noted. This creates a longer period between booking and recognized revenue. The company reported that the backlog of larger deals, those in excess of $100,000 in annual sales, was up more than 50% year-over-year.

In response to a question from an analyst about the disconnect between bookings and revenue growth, Hawkins said, "We are seeing strong demand. We're not seeing a change in the competitive environment or our win rates, and we're pleased with that," adding that the company sees a "long-term double-digit opportunity to drive revenue."

For its full-year outlook, Waystar management forecasted revenue of $1.277 billion to $1.287 billion, with a midpoint of $1.282 billion. Adjusted EBITDA is expected to be between $543 million and $549 million for fiscal 2026.

The company expects slower, near-term revenue growth, forecasting fourth-quarter revenue of approximately $323 million, representing growth of about 6%.

Ryan Daniels, group head of healthcare technology and services at William Blair, wrote in an analyst note that Waystar delivered strong results on both the top and bottom line. "We continue to expect solid organic growth going forward. While investor focus may turn to the very modest (0.2%) reduction in sales guidance, we believe strong profitability, solid bookings performance, and robust free cash flows will continue to lead the stock higher over time; we maintain our Outperform rating," he wrote.

Daniels wrote that Waystar remains a "category leader in end-to-end RCM software... leveraging its competitive position and scale advantages to enhance the platform with innovations that drive client value. Moreover, we believe innovation momentum is driving an uptick in pipeline activity, size, and bookings performance, highlighted by a continuation of strong win rates and an uptick in larger deal sizes."

Daniels also noted that concerns over AI risks and "end-market noise," such as weaker healthcare volumes and Medicaid and ACA exchange lives moving to uninsured status, are "overblown."

Waystar is positioned to capitalize on the AI-enabled transformation of RCM via stronger pricing, an expanding total addressable market and increased value-add for clients, he said. "We continue to view the sales model as highly recurring (and visible) and do not anticipate any major AI-related competitive disruption as providers continue to turn toward trusted and fully integrated partners for RCM solutions," Daniels wrote.
